c.tagline: The world's smallest island republic on a coral atoll.

taxi.fareNote: No meters; fares are negotiated in advance, typically AUD 10-20 for short intra-island trips.

emergency.medical: 111 (ambulance); Republic of Nauru (RON) Hospital is the island's only hospital)
emergency.note: 112 is also used as a general emergency number; serious medical cases are often medevaced to Australia.

english.label: Easy to get by in English

hood_desc: Nauru's seat of government, home to Parliament House, the administrative offices and the airport; suits business travelers, officials and those wanting to be near government and transit hubs.
The island's compact commercial hub with the boat harbour, banks, shops and the tallest building in Nauru; suits budget travelers and anyone wanting walkable access to services.

Nauru's south-eastern coastal district, about fifteen minutes' drive from the airport and a short walk from Anibare Bay, the island's best swimming beach. It holds the Menen Hotel, the largest on the island at 119 rooms, with Nauru's only bar.

A north-western coastal district built around the Capelle & Partner complex, which puts Nauru's main supermarket, a bakery, a coffee shop and a Bendigo Bank branch under the same roof as the serviced apartments of Ewa Lodge, a minute from Ewa beach. Self-catering and convenient, with a free airport shuttle.

water.note: Water relies on desalination and rainwater catchment with inconsistent quality; use bottled water.

transit.pay: Cash only in Australian dollars, paid directly to the driver; exact change is appreciated.
transit.hours: Irregular daytime service only, roughly hourly; no scheduled night service.
transit.note: Nauru has no metro, tram or train network; most residents and visitors rely on private cars, taxis or hotel transfers, with only an informal community bus circling the 19 km ring road.

bus: Informal community ring-road bus (no fixed schedule)

tip.r: Tipping is not customary in Nauruan culture; hotels, restaurants and taxis neither expect nor require it.

food.name: Coconut fish
food.desc: Nauru's staple plate: fresh reef fish or tuna simmered in thick coconut cream with onion and a little chilli, served with rice or boiled taro.

places.name: Menen Hotel restaurant
places.note: The island's main hotel dining room and the most consistent kitchen in Nauru.

places.name: Od'n Aiwo Hotel restaurant
places.note: Menu runs from Nauruan dishes to Chinese and European; handy for the port and Yaren.

places.name: Family eateries near the government buildings
places.note: Small home kitchens serve local plates cheaply; hours are irregular, so go early.

food.name: Ika (raw fish in citrus)
food.desc: Tuna or reef fish diced and cured in lime or lemon juice, then dressed with coconut cream, onion and cucumber; the island's version of ceviche.

places.name: Menen Hotel restaurant
places.note: Serves raw-fish plates when the boats have been out; ask what came in that day.

places.name: Anibare Harbour
places.note: Fishermen sell tuna and reef fish straight off the boats at the small boat harbour.

places.name: Family eateries near the government buildings
places.note: Local cooks prepare ika for takeaway lunches; portions are generous.

food.name: Grilled tuna and reef fish
food.desc: Skipjack and yellowfin from the waters that fund the country, plus reef fish caught off the terraces, grilled over coals with lime and salt.

places.name: Anibare Harbour
places.note: Landing point for small boats; buy whole fish and get it cooked at a nearby kitchen.

places.name: Menen Hotel restaurant
places.note: Grilled catch of the day is the safest bet on the menu, with a sea-facing terrace.

places.name: Capelle and Partner
places.note: Nauru's biggest store and eatery complex; a dependable stop for a cooked fish meal.

food.name: Buada Lagoon milkfish
food.desc: Milkfish raised in the freshwater Buada Lagoon and in inland ponds, a Nauruan tradition going back generations; usually fried or baked whole.

places.name: Buada Lagoon
places.note: Families around the lagoon still farm ibija; ask locally about buying fish.

places.name: Menen Hotel restaurant
places.note: Puts local milkfish on the menu when supply allows; ask the kitchen.

places.name: Capelle and Partner
places.note: Sells local and frozen fish alongside its restaurant counter.

food.name: Pandanus and coconut sweets
food.desc: Pandanus fruit cooked down into a dark, sticky paste, plus coconut and banana puddings; the traditional sweet side of a Nauruan feast.

places.name: Family eateries near the government buildings
places.note: Home-made puddings appear on counters; best chance to try pandanus preparations.

places.name: Community feasts and church gatherings
places.note: Traditional sweets are made for Angam Day and church events; visitors are usually welcomed.

places.name: Menen Hotel restaurant
places.note: Occasional local desserts alongside the standard international sweets.

food.name: Imported staples
food.desc: Worth knowing: with little farmland, most food is shipped in. Corned beef, rice, instant noodles and tinned fish are the everyday Nauruan table.

places.name: Capelle and Partner
places.note: The island's main supermarket; stock depends on when the last ship docked.

places.name: Ring road takeaways
places.note: Chinese-run takeaways along the coast road do rice and noodle plates late into the evening.

places.name: Od'n Aiwo Hotel restaurant
places.note: Reliable if shops are bare; the kitchen keeps a longer menu than most places.

food.name: Fresh drinking coconut
food.desc: Green coconuts cut open on the spot; the water is the island's everyday thirst-quencher and the soft jelly inside is eaten with a shard of the husk.

places.name: Roadside stands, ring road
places.note: Vendors sell drinking nuts along the coast road, cheapest near the beaches.

places.name: Anibare Harbour
places.note: Easy to find coconuts beside the harbour and beach picnic area.

places.name: Capelle and Partner
places.note: Sells coconuts and cold drinks when roadside sellers are not out.

food.name: Coconut toddy
food.desc: Sap tapped from the coconut flower and drunk fresh and sweet in the morning or left to ferment into a sour, mildly alcoholic palm wine.

places.name: Village tappers, Buada and Anabar
places.note: Toddy is tapped at dawn in the villages; ask locally rather than expecting a shop.

places.name: Menen Hotel bar
places.note: Main bar on the island for cold beer and spirits, busiest at weekends.

places.name: Od'n Aiwo Hotel bar
places.note: Casual bar near the port; a good place to ask about local toddy.

landmarks: Nauru Parliament House
The modest seat of government for the world's smallest island nation, located in Yaren District, Nauru's de facto capital — a quirky must-see for anyone collecting the world's least-visited capitals.
Command Ridge

The highest point on Nauru, this coral pinnacle was a Japanese military lookout during WWII and still holds rusting artillery guns and bunkers amid panoramic views over the phosphate-scarred interior and turquoise coastline.
Buada Lagoon
A tranquil freshwater lagoon ringed by lush vegetation and banana palms, offering a surprising splash of green calm in contrast to Nauru's mined-out limestone pinnacles.
Anibare Bay
A picture-perfect curve of golden sand and clear water on the island's east coast, popular for swimming, picnics, and watching local fishermen cast their lines at sunset.
Moqua Well and Caves
A dramatic limestone cave system with a subterranean freshwater pool, once Nauru's primary water source — an eerie, atmospheric detour for adventurous travelers.
Nauru Phosphate Pinnacles (Topside)
The moonlike, jagged limestone formations left behind by a century of phosphate mining across the island's interior plateau — a stark, otherworldly landscape found just outside Yaren.
Yaren District Airstrip and WWII Relics
Nauru's sole runway sits alongside rusting Japanese fortifications and gun emplacements, remnants of the island's occupation during the Second World War.
Nauru's Coastal Ring Road
The 19-kilometer coastal road encircling the island passes near Yaren and offers a scenic, breezy drive or bike ride with the Pacific Ocean on one side almost the entire way.
Nauru Secondary School War Memorial
A small but poignant memorial near Yaren commemorating Nauruans who suffered deportation and hardship under Japanese occupation during WWII.
Nauru's Coral Coastline near Yaren
Dramatic wave-battered coral cliffs and tide pools line the shore around Yaren, ideal for photographing the raw power of the surrounding Pacific Ocean.

train.note: Nauru has a short industrial railway built to carry phosphate to the port, but it has never carried passengers and is largely disused. Arrive by air into Nauru International Airport on Nauru Airlines flights from Brisbane, Nadi and the Micronesian islands.

bus.note: No international coaches. A free government bus circles the 19 km ring road around the island a few times a day, which is the entire public transport network. Most residents drive; the island can be circumnavigated in about half an hour.

ferry.note: There is no scheduled passenger ferry to or from Nauru - the island has no harbour, and even cargo ships must moor offshore and be unloaded by lighter because of the reef. All passenger travel is by air.
